title: What Each Profile Can Decide
scopeNote: This keeps the judgement grid, which is the inferential mechanism rather than a quiz: for each claim and each profile the learner says whether it supports, counts against, or cannot decide. A third claim, further profiles, and the step from a single to a double dissociation worked through explicitly stay in the longer version.
summary: Two claims about memory and three fictional profiles, judged in every combination. One profile has both abilities impaired and is included precisely because it decides nothing.
learningObjectives: Judge whether a case supports a claim, counts against it, or cannot decide it.
Explain why a profile with everything impaired is uninformative about separability.
Explain what a single dissociation leaves open and what a double one closes.
Recognise that identifying an undecidable pairing is a finding rather than a failure.
Distinguish evidence about separate systems from evidence about task difficulty.
interactionTypes: three fictional profiles stated as evidence with both abilities summarised
six judgements across two claims and three profiles
three answers per cell, the third being cannot decide
an explanation for every cell whether right or wrong
a summary that scores the cannot-decide cells separately
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout, with every judgement a labelled button marked with a glyph and a hidden note as well as a colour. Each profile card states both abilities in words as well as in prose, and every judgement row repeats that summary next to the options, so the evidence never has to be held in mind or scrolled back to. A reason appears for every cell whether the answer was right or wrong, and progress is announced through a polite live region. Nothing is timed and there is no motion.
dataStatus: Three fictional profiles described in a sentence each. No syndrome is named and no real patient is described.
simulationNotes: Profile A has new facts lost and skill learning preserved; Profile B is the opposite; Profile C has both lost. A and B together form a double dissociation, which also answers the reply that the lost task was simply harder. C is present precisely because it is uninformative: both lost is what one shared system predicts and also what two separate systems predict if both are damaged, so it fits either way. The summary scores the three cannot-decide cells separately from the rest, because a learner who marks them as supporting the claim has made exactly the mistake the activity is for.
readmeTopic: which claims a case can settle, and which it cannot settle however severe it is
